name: Rip rap
seoDesc: Rip rap: work out gravitational acceleration (g) from the water velocity and the specific gravity. A free construction calculator with the formula, units…
summary: gravitational acceleration (g) is what the Rip rap calculator works out, and it gets there from the water velocity, the specific gravity, the average rock diameter and the depth. That makes it useful for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Rip rap calculator work?
sections.html:
The Rip rap calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports gravitational acceleration (g) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the isbash constant (C)); then you type in the water velocity (V), the specific gravity (S), the average rock diameter (D₅₀) and the depth.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Rip rap calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Gravitational acceleration (g)=(1 ÷ 2) × (water velocity (V) ^ 2) ÷ ((isbash constant (C) ^ 2) × average rock diameter (D₅₀) × (specific gravity (S) − 1))
Area=volume ÷ depth
Volume=100 × total volume ÷ (wastage + 100)
Weight=density × total volume
Rip rap rock cost=price per weight × weight

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in meters per second squared, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.
  • Shown in square meters, and convertible to any of the 24 units on that chip.
  • Shown in cubic meters, and convertible to any of the 40 units on that chip.
  • Shown in metric tons, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.
  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • %, opening in percent
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Rip rap calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the water velocity, the specific gravity and the average rock diameter — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Rip rap calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns gravitational acceleration (g), derived from the water velocity, the specific gravity and the average rock diameter. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Rip rap calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the water velocity, the specific gravity, the average rock diameter and the depth, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter water velocity (V) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Water velocity (V) opens in meters per second and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Rip rap calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
